name: mined
title: Mined AI-slop tells
description: Every tell this project mined itself, in one set. The two shipped sets are ports of other people's work and stay separate; these were gathered from published research, style guides and other detectors, then measured against a matched human/AI corpus. Each rule records where it came from in `from` and `source`, and what it scored in `evidence`. The full survey is in research/log.md and the measurements in research/audit.md.

rules.name: Em dash
rules.description: An em dash, or an en dash or double hyphen standing in for one. Every occurrence, no threshold.
rules.suggest: A comma if the aside is light, a colon if what follows explains, brackets if it is a true aside, a full stop if it is really a second sentence.
rules.measured: This rule is a style preference, deliberately kept separate from the detection research. Four independent measurements agree the em dash does NOT distinguish machine prose from human prose: sloptells found acclaimed human writing uses more of them than models do (0.67 against 0.56 per 1000 characters); The Economist found only Claude above the human rate, with ChatGPT markedly below; humanizer-de states that a single em dash proves nothing; and this project's own corpus agreed. None of that is an argument for keeping them in your own writing, which is a different question and yours to answer.

hit: The migration took a week — longer than anyone expected.
It shipped on a Tuesday – quietly, as these things do.
The queue ran clean -- for four months at least.
miss: The study ran from 1990–1995 without a break.
It is a well-known problem in the parser.
Run it with --force to install anyway.

rules.evidence: On the audit corpus: 40 hits in 8/18 human documents, 0 in 0/18 AI documents.
rules.note: Ships on where the mined set is loaded at all, because it is a house-style preference rather than a detection claim. See `measured` for what the research actually says about em dashes, which is the opposite.

rules.name: Too few commas
rules.description: LLM prose uses fewer commas than human prose. The Economist compared 55,940 sentences of its own journalism, CNN, the New York Times, the Washington Post and novels from 1950 to 2022 against four models rewriting the same articles, and found the models short of commas, semicolons and parentheses alike.
rules.suggest: No single sentence is wrong. The document as a whole reads as a run of flat declaratives; vary the shapes.

hit: The system reads the file. It parses each line into a record. The records go to a queue. A worker takes them off the queue. It validates them. Invalid records are logged and dropped. Valid records go to the database. The database applies them in order. Each batch is committed together. If a batch fails the whole batch is retried. After three failures the batch moves to a dead letter queue. An operator reviews that queue every morning. Most entries turn out to be malformed input. They come from one upstream partner. We opened a ticket with them in March. The ticket is still open. We now reject their malformed records at the edge instead. That reduced the dead letter volume by ninety percent. The remaining failures are genuine bugs on our side. We fix them as they appear. The edge rejection was a fifteen line change. It shipped on a Tuesday afternoon. Nobody noticed it. The operator stopped getting paged at six in the morning. She sent a message to say so. That message is pinned in the channel. It is the only performance review that change will ever get. rules.description: Three or more consecutive sentences built on the same syntactic frame, with different words in the slots. rules.note: A crude stand-in for part-of-speech tagging, which this engine does not have. rules.description: The wistful closer. Both halves ship as separate entries in the phrase list, which is how often they co-occur.
rules.suggest: End on the last real thing that happened.

hit: Maybe, just maybe, they would make it.
It was not much, but for now, that was enough.
And maybe that was enough.
miss: Maybe we should leave.
That was enough rope to reach the branch.

rules.name: “They would face it together”
rules.description: The resolve-and-embrace ending, which resolves nothing.
rules.suggest: Let the last scene stand without a summary of how everyone felt about it.

hit: Whatever came next, they would face it together.

rules.name: “Something else entirely”
rules.description: Withholding as a substitute for description: the thing is named only as not-the-other-thing.
rules.suggest: Name it. If it cannot be named yet, describe what the character can actually perceive.

hit: This was something else entirely.
There was something darker behind the door.
It was unlike anything she had ever seen.
